peer_critiques.critique: FATAL as specified. A wrapper is a control only if it is the sole path to the capability, and nothing in this runtime interposes it. The PreToolUse hook has exactly two verbs — its own header states 'exit 2 at L38 denies the tool call. The only mechanism in this repo that can stop an action.' Deny and allow. It cannot rewrite mcp__higgsfield__tiktok_publish into wrapper.publish(hash). There is no redirect, shim or proxy; an MCP call goes model-to-server and a repo-owned wrapper sits BESIDE that path, not on it. So the wrapper is chosen by the agent, not imposed on it, and an agent holding both the wrapper and the direct tool under a done-test and a stall ceiling at 3am calls the direct tool. The grant does not stop it either: measured this round, this dispatch path hands out tiktok_publish, Gmail send_message and sandbox_exec with no agent file, no policy entry, zero MCP permission rules, and exit 0 with empty stderr from the live hook. That makes P5 the fifth entry on a list whose own P3 ranks built-and-never-wired as the TOP risk, and P3's stated reason applies to it exactly — a wrapper nothing routes through is indistinguishable from absence and worse than absence, because the founder will believe outbound is two-step when it is one. WHAT WOULD HAVE TO BE TRUE FOR IT TO SURVIVE: the direct tools must be unreachable, not merely deprecated. Three conditions, the third load-bearing. (1) The grant is removed from the pack — necessary and measured insufficient, because this path grants what no file granted. (2) permissions.deny gains MCP globs — currently zero, and whether deny binds inside a dispatched subagent is their own first open question, unresolved; Rule 10 applies to their design as they applied it to resolvers, so unresolved never pass. (3) The loop body is launched with the direct outbound tools struck from the roster: claude -p --disallowedTools exists on the binary here and is the only mechanism I can find that makes a wrapper the sole remaining path, because it removes the alternative rather than discouraging it. With (3) P5 becomes the strongest item on their list and I would rank it above their reach axis, because it converts a policy into a physics. Note what this is not: it does not attack volume, which they already conceded ('build three controls, not thirteen'), and it does not attack ordering, which they explicitly did not concede. It says one of the three survivors has nothing making it binding.

The clause carrying the decisive weight is falsified on one live path. P8 refuses worker trust and calls the third reason decisive: 'the grant is already the security boundary — an agent cannot research its way into holding a tool it was not granted.' True on the Agent(subagent_type:) path; false on the path that dispatched this board. I did not research my way into holding tiktok_publish, sandbox_exec, Gmail send_message and an authenticated Chrome — I was handed all fifteen servers, by no file, with no log line, while exactly two agent files in the repository declare mcpServers and each declares one server. The refusal of worker trust may still be right: the volume argument and the no-persistent-subject argument stand on their own and I do not dispute either. What I dispute is that the grant CLOSES gap #10. It closes it on one path. Until the dispatch-path census exists, 'the grant is the whole trust model' is a statement whose truth value varies by how the worker was launched, and nobody currently knows how many launchers there are.

Their own strongest_counter concedes the world resolver may report unresolved for eighteen months. It does not concede the structural consequence, which is worse than slowness: four components — trust, bandit allocation, cost-per-surviving-artifact, the company metric — are sequenced strictly behind a resolver that Rule 10 REQUIRES to return unresolved whenever it cannot check. Those four therefore have no build trigger at all. That is not a forced order; it is a stall dressed as a dependency, and this repo has already logged the failure mode: three verified_by: judge claims with empty panels resolving unresolved forever, recorded in CLAUDE.md as possibly structurally unresolvable in this runtime. The repair sits inside their own counter and should be promoted out of it — build the archive (P7) and the field store (P6) IN PARALLEL with the world resolver rather than downstream of it, and accept that trust is not built in year one. Their P5 preference corpus and P6 global FIELDS are the two things that compound at n=1 with no third-party auth and no power calculation, and both are currently placed behind an instrument that cannot fire.

The rule as written forbids the birth certificate that three other lanes rank first. 'No new step enters the 48-step check suite unless it fails on a defect found in work that is not about the harness' — but risk-modeler:P3 ranks the birth certificate first of everything and specifies it as 'a step in scripts/lib/check-suite.js', visionary:P10 endorses it, and my own P8 proposes its predicate. It is a new step and the defect it catches is a harness defect by definition, so it can never satisfy the trigger. Three of five personas want a thing the fourth's rule makes unbuildable, and the board should notice that before the Synthesizer has to. The concern behind P5 is right and its ratio is the most alarming number anyone produced (30,446 test lines against 16,839 producing lines; STEPS.length re-verified at 48 this round, EXCLUDED at 10). The narrower collision — with the stall-counter fix and symmetric Rule 10 — is smaller than it looks, because those are edits to existing files rather than new steps, and I say so rather than scoring off it.

A compounds: flywheel|feeder|inventory field that nothing falsifies is precisely mcpServers across 52 agent files while no MCP configuration existed anywhere — fifty-two declarations, zero grants, and schema-lint.js now fails any declaration no configuration backs, which is the shape the fix must take here too. The first convening of the board is simultaneously this repo's most permissive dispatch and its least documented one. remaining_dissent.holds_because: MEASUREMENTS PRECEDE CONTROLS. Between them these two lanes place roughly thirteen mechanisms before an unattended run. Sorted by cost to reverse, exactly one is unbounded — identity on the row — and exactly one more is free to honour, inbound after outbound. The rest are files, and a file is git revert. The dissent is not that the controls are wrong; four of them I would build. It is about what earns the right to PRECEDE, and my answer is unchanged: cost to reverse, plus the silent-and-compounding class I added this round. On that test, four of the five controls placed first are aimed at a boundary nobody has characterised — the grant — and building a control against an uncharacterised boundary is how you get the fifth unwired mechanism. The two measurements I put first cost an agent's minutes, compete with the founder for nothing, and make the controls afterwards SMALLER: a census that finds one leaky launcher turns 'build a wrapper, a register, a rate ceiling and a reach axis' into 'stop launching workers on that path'.

'Keep L1' is one decision over two components with different reach, and the two peers who touched L1 treated it as one object while pointing in opposite directions over the seam. The Strategist says keep L1 unchanged and stop growing it; the Visionary says point the ledger's forced expiry at every store. Both are reasonable and they are about DIFFERENT HALVES. The claim ledger's unit is an assertion — it follows the system into video, pricing, copy and outbound work, and the Visionary is right that it should govern more. scripts/verdict.mjs binds subject = sha256(git diff); a published video, a sent email, a live landing page and a price change have no diff, therefore no subject, therefore no verdict record, and it cannot follow the system anywhere the Adversary's demand test would take it. Nobody engaged with this and the first non-code mission discovers it by shipping. It is one sentence to state in the design now and a surprise later, and it is precisely the kind of seam this framing asked me to name: two subsystems meeting under one decision and disagreeing silently.

I ACCEPT the demand test and dissent only from the tripwire's blanket form. The test is the cleanest instrument anyone proposed, costs hours rather than weeks, removes the machine from the experiment entirely and therefore actually tests demand; it is better than the synthetic-mission counter-methodology I offered in Round 1. But the tripwire — zero commits under .claude|scripts|docs in BOTH repositories for seven days — does not only cost seven days of harness polish, which I agree should stop. It costs seven days of the two cheapest items in the building, neither of which is founder work and neither of which is a mechanism. First, the task id: all five of us named it from four framings, and the Adversary reached it from the opposite direction — their own sixth open question asks what the 858 commits cost and answers 'unanswerable in BOTH directions, including mine' for want of a task id that survives a session. The tripwire forbids for a week the field that would make the demand test's own cost accounting possible. Second, the dispatch-path census: seven more days of dispatches on a path that hands out sandbox_exec and mail-send with no record. Both are agent-minutes and neither touches the founder's hours, which is the resource the base-rate argument says is scarce. The ban is right about mechanisms and wrong about measurements. Exempt the two, run the test, and record the exemption as a dated .out-of-scope entry rather than a verbal carve-out, per strategist:P4.

updated_positions.claim: REVISED. Cost to reverse drives sequencing, and the bill of materials splits into THREE classes, not two: irreversible, silent-and-compounding, and everything else.
updated_positions.reasoning: Unbounded to reverse: identity on the row, because history written without the column is permanently unattributable. Not reversible at all: anything outbound — git revert does not unsend an email or unpublish a video, which is ADR-001's own test — and, per revised P11, anything that GRANTS an outbound tool. The new middle class comes from risk-modeler:P3: a control that fails toward passing, or one that exists and is not in the path of the action it names, is cheap to git revert and expensive to have believed, because the founder will believe the system is bounded when it is not. My P4 is the canonical instance. Cheap and loud, days: personas, council, board, missions file, balcony views, FIELDS. The operating rule: reversible-and-loud is built fast, loose and continuously, matching the founder's cadence and Omnigent's fifteen releases in ten weeks with 'Phase N' appearing nowhere; reversible-and-SILENT is built correctly or not at all, because half-built it is negative value; and only the first class earns the right to precede everything.

The census is: for each live dispatch path — Agent(subagent_type:), the teammate path, claude -p with and without --allowedTools, and the mission-control dispatch — record the delivered tool roster and whether Workflow is in it, and register the result as a ledger claim with an expiry, because a fact about a runtime that ships every two weeks is exactly what rule 9 exists for. It is forced not by irreversibility but because it is the cheapest thing that changes what gets built afterwards: if one launcher leaks and the others do not, the correct response is not a wrapper, a named-human register, a rate ceiling and a reach axis — it is to stop launching workers on that path, which is a configuration change and not a subsystem. The honest weakness, and it is adversary:P6's: a census is another claim that will expire and need a disposition, and I have just argued for the ninth instrument in a repo whose problem is instruments. The narrow defence is that this is the first one aimed at a boundary rather than at a statement, and the only one that can remove work.

strongest_counter: My Round-1 counter was that I had described a better truth machine and the founder said the truth machine was the mistake. Two rounds later that counter is stronger, not weaker, and it now carries numbers from two lanes that could not see each other: the Adversary's base rate (eleven projects over twenty commits, nine dead, median about three weeks, this repo on day twenty-two with a velocity signature indistinguishable from two dead ventures) and the Strategist's ratio (30,446 lines of test code against 16,839 of producing script, six mechanisms of ~420). I have responded by cutting my forced list from six items to two, which is the right direction and may not be far enough. But the sharper counter against my Round-2 position is a different one, and it comes from my own headline finding. I have just argued that the most load-bearing fact in the building is that the tool grant does not bind — and my remedy is a CENSUS, which is an instrument, which is the ninth instrument this repo would build. adversary:P6 is the general form and I cannot dismiss it: every artifact is a claim, every claim needs an expiry, every expiry needs a disposition, every disposition is another artifact, and a fact about a runtime that ships every two weeks will expire fast and loudly. So my second forced item is, by my own peers' argument, more harness work — proposed by the persona whose framing is the bill of materials, in a meeting convened because the bill of materials had eaten the company. I do not have a clean answer. The narrow defence is that this particular instrument has a property none of the other eight has: it can REMOVE work. If the census finds that one launcher leaks and the others do not, the correct response is not a wrapper, a register, a rate ceiling and a reach axis — it is to stop using that launcher, a configuration change rather than a subsystem, and that would delete four proposals from this board's list rather than adding a fifth. That is why I still put it before the controls rather than beside them. The weaker half, said plainly: if the census comes back clean on every path, I have spent an afternoon and built nothing, and the Adversary was right that the demand test should have had the afternoon. What makes this a fair test rather than a hedge is that the two outcomes are distinguishable in advance and the measurement takes minutes, which is more than can be said for anything else on the table.
